title: The Extent of Hellenic Culture
summary: Greek religion, language, and culture spread far beyond the Greek mainland through centuries of colonization and, later, the conquests of Alexander the Great. It reached from the western Mediterranean to Central Asia and shaped, and was shaped by, the cultures it encountered.

key_aspects.title: Archaic-era colonization
key_aspects.description: Beginning around the 8th century BCE, Greek city-states founded colonies across the Mediterranean and Black Sea coasts. These included Magna Graecia in southern Italy and Sicily, settlements along Ionia (western Asia Minor), and outposts on the Black Sea coast. The colonies carried Greek religious practice, temple architecture, and civic institutions with them.

key_aspects.title: Alexander the Great and the Hellenistic period
key_aspects.description: Alexander's conquests in the 4th century BCE (334–323 BCE) rapidly extended Greek political control from Egypt through the former Persian Empire into Central Asia and northwestern India. Greek language and culture spread with this expansion, inaugurating what historians call the Hellenistic period.

key_aspects.title: Hellenistic kingdoms
key_aspects.description: After Alexander's death, his empire fractured into successor kingdoms ruled by his former generals: Ptolemaic Egypt (based in Alexandria, a major center of Greek scholarship), the Seleucid Empire (spanning much of the former Persian territory), and others. These kingdoms actively promoted Greek culture among local elites while also absorbing local religious and artistic traditions.

key_aspects.title: Koine Greek and cultural exchange
key_aspects.description: A common form of Greek, Koine, became a lingua franca across the Hellenistic world, used in administration, trade, and scholarship far beyond Greece itself. Cultural exchange ran in both directions. Greek art and religious iconography absorbed influences from Egyptian, Persian, and Central Asian traditions, producing distinctive hybrid styles such as Greco-Buddhist art in the region of ancient Gandhara.

key_aspects.title: Roman adoption of Greek religion and culture
key_aspects.description: As Rome's power grew and eventually absorbed the Hellenistic kingdoms, Roman religion and culture extensively adopted and adapted Greek gods, myths, and artistic conventions. Most Olympian gods gained direct Roman equivalents, such as Zeus and Jupiter or Aphrodite and Venus. Greek literature and philosophy became central to elite Roman education.
